title: Field Masks: Remove Redundant Paths Before Fetching
sourceTitle: Netflix TechBlog: Practical API Design, Part 1 — Protobuf FieldMask
sourceNote: Original exercise based on Netflix engineering documentation, not a published interview question. All paths are assumed schema-valid; no repeated fields or wildcards are included. An explicitly present empty mask selects nothing here; an absent mask is outside this contract.
prompt: Normalize an explicitly present field mask. Each dot-separated path segment matches [a-z_][a-z0-9_]*. Remove duplicates and any path covered by a selected ancestor. Return the remaining paths and their distinct top-level fields, both sorted lexicographically. Selecting schedule includes schedule.date, but does not include schedule_dates.
approach: Insert paths into a trie keyed by whole field-name segments. A terminal node selects its entire subtree, so stop when an existing terminal is reached.
When a new path ends, mark that node terminal and discard its descendants. This handles parents that arrive after children; dots, not raw character prefixes, determine ancestry.
Enumerate terminal paths, sort them, and extract distinct first segments. Use these top-level selections to decide which dependent services are needed before fetching their data.
complexity: Expected O(C + K log K · L) time with hashed trie children, where C is total input characters, K output paths, and L maximum path length; O(C) auxiliary space including trie and output.
pitfalls: A raw prefix test incorrectly treats schedule_dates as a child of schedule.
Filtering the response after fetching every field does not avoid remote calls.
followUp: How would descriptor validation reject an unknown field or a repeated field in a nonfinal path position?
answer: The first example reduces to [schedule,scripts,title], so only those three top-level fields are requested. A later parent removes an earlier descendant.

examples.explanation: The parent schedule covers its nested email field; title repeats.
The underscore keeps schedule_dates separate from schedule.
a.b covers a.b.c but not its sibling a.bc.
This contract receives a present empty mask, rather than an absent mask.

title: Shot Encoding: Choose One Representation per Byte Budget
sourceTitle: Netflix TechBlog: Dynamic Optimizer — A Perceptual Video Encoding Optimization Framework
sourceNote: Original discrete optimization exercise inspired by Netflix shot-based encoding; not a published interview question or a reproduction of its production optimizer. Integer byte costs and additive synthetic quality scores are local assumptions, not measured VMAF values.
prompt: Each shot has candidate encodes with positive integer byte costs and nonnegative integer quality scores. Choose exactly one candidate per shot, keeping total bytes at most a nonnegative integer budget B. Return the maximum total quality, or null if no complete selection fits. A shot with no candidates is infeasible; zero shots have total quality zero.
approach: Let dp[b] be the best quality using exactly b bytes after the processed shots. Initialize dp[0]=0 and all other states to negative infinity.
For each shot, create a fresh next array. For every reachable b and each candidate (c,q), update next[b+c]=max(next[b+c],dp[b]+q) when b+c<=B. Then replace dp with next.
Take the maximum reachable value over all costs at most B. A transition chooses one candidate from the current shot; separate arrays prevent selecting that shot twice or skipping it.
complexity: O((B+1) · (1+n+sum_i k_i)) time for n shots with k_i candidates in shot i, and O(B+1) auxiliary space. This is pseudopolynomial in the numeric budget, not polynomial in its bit length.
pitfalls: Updating one array in place can reuse a shot. Initializing every state to zero can silently skip mandatory shots.
A greedy quality-per-extra-byte upgrade can lose to an indivisible, larger upgrade.
followUp: How would you reconstruct selected encodes, or handle a budget too large for a dense array?
answer: The first example reaches quality 17 with costs 4+3+1=8. In the second, choose costs 1+4 for quality 7; choosing the best-ratio first-shot upgrade leaves quality only 5.

examples.explanation: Choose the second, second, and first candidates. No feasible complete selection has higher quality.
Choose costs 1 and 4. Upgrading the first shot uses the available budget less effectively despite a better local ratio.
The minimum complete cost is three bytes.

title: Adaptive Concurrency: Trace a Vegas Limit Update
sourceNote: Original exercise based on the pinned Netflix implementation, not a published interview question. Trace only its core update: baseline RTT is already initialized, no probe or baseline reset occurs, smoothing is one, and the explicitly configured thresholds and step functions replace defaults.
prompt: Return the limit after each sample. Start with integer limit L in [1,20], fixed baseline RTT R0=100 ms, maximum 20, and integer sample RTT R>=R0. Use the exact arithmetic model q=ceil(L(1-R0/R)). Use threshold=1, alpha=3, beta=6, increase(L)=L+1, decrease(L)=L-1. Each sample supplies R, a nonnegative integer inflight count, and boolean didDrop.
approach: Evaluate each sample against the previous limit. A drop decreases L by one first, even when demand is low. Otherwise, if 2*inflight<L, keep L unchanged.
For other samples, q<=1 adds six; otherwise q<3 adds one; q>6 subtracts one; all remaining queue estimates keep L unchanged. Equality at alpha or beta therefore holds the limit.
Clamp a changed limit to [1,20]. Apply each completed update before processing the next sample. With smoothing one and integer step functions, no fractional limit remains.
complexity: O(n) time for n samples with O(1) running state; returning every updated limit takes O(n) output space.
pitfalls: The queue estimate is not an observed queue length. Concurrency differs from requests per second.
IEEE floating-point rounding near an integer can affect ceil. This exercise uses exact arithmetic rather than claiming identical Java results for every fraction.
followUp: What changes when smoothing is fractional, or a new minimum RTT causes an early return?
answer: The six-sample trace produces [9,9,8,8,7,13]. The fourth sample is demand-limited; the fifth still backs off because a drop takes precedence.

examples.explanation: Small queue, middle band, high queue, low demand, drop, and aggressive growth respectively.
Queue estimates equal alpha=3 and beta=6; both boundaries hold.
Aggressive growth would reach 24, so the maximum clamps it to 20.
A drop cannot reduce the limit below one.
